what: Build Check Part 2 (wording check), statements version v0.2, 5 October 2026.

statements_checked.question: When can I plant or move a rose?
statements_checked.text: Plant a bare-root rose (one sold without soil on its roots) while it is dormant, with no leaves, between late autumn and early spring. One source says to avoid the middle of winter when the ground is frozen.

statements_checked.question: When can I plant or move a rose?
statements_checked.text: In New Zealand, winter is the best time to plant a rose, and roses can be planted on through spring. One garden centre says new-season roses reach the shops from June. Months are only a guide.

statements_checked.question: When can I plant or move a rose?
statements_checked.text: In Australia, plant bare-root roses in winter, while they are dormant. Two rose societies say June or July, and one source says from May. Months are only a guide.

statements_checked.question: When can I plant or move a rose?
statements_checked.text: In the UK, plant bare-root roses in late autumn, or from late winter to early spring before growth starts.

statements_checked.question: When can I plant or move a rose?
statements_checked.text: In the US, where winters are very cold, spring is the preferred time to plant bare-root roses. One source puts the line at winters that fall below -10 °F, and says that where it stays warmer than that, autumn or spring both work.

statements_checked.question: When can I plant or move a rose?
statements_checked.text: A rose in a pot can be planted over a longer season than a bare-root rose. UK and New Zealand sources say all year, and two US sources say through the growing season.
statements_checked.limit: One source says not to plant into frozen or very dry ground. Another says to keep it well watered if you plant in spring or summer. One says autumn or winter is still the best time.

statements_checked.question: When can I plant or move a rose?
statements_checked.text: Move an established rose while it is dormant, which means it is not actively growing. Most sources say winter. Some say late autumn or early spring.

statements_checked.question: When can I plant or move a rose?
statements_checked.text: In New Zealand, one garden centre says the best time to move a rose is after pruning in July, while it is dormant, and once the risk of frost has passed. Months are only a guide.

statements_checked.question: When can I plant or move a rose?
statements_checked.text: A rose can be moved in the growing season if you have to. It will need extra watering afterwards.

statements_checked.question: Where should I plant a rose?
statements_checked.text: Choose a sunny spot. Sources give a minimum of four to six hours of direct sun a day.

statements_checked.question: Where should I plant a rose?
statements_checked.text: Roses need soil that drains well. Where the soil is heavy or drains poorly, some sources suggest a raised bed or mound, and others suggest digging in gypsum or compost.

statements_checked.question: Where should I plant a rose?
statements_checked.text: Keep roses away from the roots of nearby trees and shrubs, which compete with them.

statements_checked.question: Where should I plant a rose?
statements_checked.text: How far apart to plant depends on the type of rose and how big it will grow, so check the label. Where sources give a distance, it is about 50 cm to 1 m (20 inches to 3 feet). One gives 75 to 90 cm (2½ to 3 feet) for hybrid tea roses.

statements_checked.question: Where should I plant a rose?
statements_checked.text: A new rose planted where a rose grew before may struggle to establish and may grow poorly. One source suggests choosing a spot where roses haven't grown.

statements_checked.question: How do I plant a rose?
statements_checked.text: Plant a bare-root rose (one sold without soil on its roots) soon after you get it, and don't let its roots dry out.

statements_checked.question: How do I plant a rose?
statements_checked.text: If you can't plant a bare-root rose straight away, keep it in its packaging somewhere cool and safe from frost. One source allows up to two weeks, with the roots kept moist, and another up to three weeks.

statements_checked.question: How do I plant a rose?
statements_checked.text: Soak the roots of a bare-root rose in water before planting.

statements_checked.question: How do I plant a rose?
statements_checked.text: Soak a bare-root rose's roots for anywhere from one hour to 24 hours before planting. Sources differ within that range. Two say not to soak for longer than 24 hours, and one of them says it may damage the roots.

statements_checked.question: How do I plant a rose?
statements_checked.text: Trim off any damaged or broken roots before planting. One source says not to cut healthy roots to make them fit, but to dig a bigger hole.

statements_checked.question: How do I plant a rose?
statements_checked.text: Dig the planting hole wider than the roots. Several sources say about twice as wide.

statements_checked.question: How do I plant a rose?
statements_checked.text: For a bare-root rose, make a mound of soil in the bottom of the hole and spread the roots over it.

statements_checked.question: How do I plant a rose?
statements_checked.text: Plant a potted rose at the same depth it was growing in its pot. Advice on where the bud union (the knobbly join near the base where the rose was grafted) should sit differs, so check that too.

statements_checked.question: How do I plant a rose?
statements_checked.text: Water the rose in well as soon as it is planted.

statements_checked.question: How do I plant a rose?
statements_checked.text: Experts disagree on whether to prune a bare-root rose at planting. Some cut the stems back when they plant. One source says a packaged rose has already been pruned and rarely needs more, and another prunes in the first winter after planting.

statements_checked.question: How deep should I plant the bud union?
statements_checked.text: Experts disagree on how deep to plant the bud union (the knobbly join near the base where the rose was grafted). Advice ranges from up to 5 cm (2 inches) above the soil, to level with it, to as much as 10 cm (4 inches) below. Sources that give a reason for burying it are speaking of places with cold winters, and say it protects the rose from the cold. Two sources give reasons against burying it: a reported risk of dieback, and, in mild climates, disease at the union.

statements_checked.question: How deep should I plant the bud union?
statements_checked.text: In New Zealand and Australia, plant the bud union (the knobbly join near the base where the rose was grafted) level with the soil or up to 5 cm above it.

statements_checked.question: How deep should I plant the bud union?
statements_checked.text: In the UK, sources differ on the bud union (the knobbly join near the base where the rose was grafted). One says to plant it at soil level, not below, because burying it is reported to raise the risk of dieback. A UK rose nursery sets it about 5 cm below the soil when replanting a rose.

statements_checked.question: How deep should I plant the bud union?
statements_checked.text: In the US, extension sources in places with cold winters plant the bud union (the knobbly join near the base where the rose was grafted) below the soil, from slightly below to 4 inches (about 10 cm) down. In one mild area, one source plants it an inch above. Ask your local extension service what is done where you live.

statements_checked.question: How deep should I plant the bud union?
statements_checked.text: I couldn't find advice on how deep to plant the bud union in New Zealand's colder districts. A local rose society is the place to ask.

statements_checked.question: Can I plant a rose where another rose grew?
statements_checked.text: A new rose planted where a rose grew before may struggle to establish and may grow poorly. This is called replant disease.

statements_checked.question: Can I plant a rose where another rose grew?
statements_checked.text: If you plant in the same spot, swap the soil in the planting hole for fresh soil from another part of the garden. Sources differ on how much to take out: from two buckets of soil, along with the old rose's roots, to a hole 45 to 60 cm across and 30 to 45 cm deep. One source gives planting somewhere else as another option.

statements_checked.question: Can I plant a rose where another rose grew?
statements_checked.text: Experts disagree about replant disease. Several advise replacing the soil. One rose specialist calls that the old method and instead adds compost or well-rotted manure and treats the new rose with mycorrhizal fungi. That source reports that opinion is divided on whether the problem is real.

statements_checked.question: Can I plant a rose where another rose grew?
statements_checked.text: I couldn't find a comparison of which remedy for replant disease works best in a home garden. A local rose society is the place to ask.

statements_checked.question: How do I move an established rose?
statements_checked.text: Move an established rose while it is dormant, which means it is not actively growing. Most sources say winter. Some say late autumn or early spring.

statements_checked.question: How do I move an established rose?
statements_checked.text: In New Zealand, one garden centre says the best time to move a rose is after pruning in July, while it is dormant, and once the risk of frost has passed. Months are only a guide.

statements_checked.question: How do I move an established rose?
statements_checked.text: Cut the top growth back before a winter move. Sources differ on how much, from cutting it back by a third to cutting it down to about 30 cm (12 inches).

statements_checked.question: How do I move an established rose?
statements_checked.text: Dig wide around the rose and keep as many of the roots as you can. Sources give different distances, from about 25 cm (10 inches) out from the base to as much as 60 cm (24 inches), and one says the larger the better.

statements_checked.question: How do I move an established rose?
statements_checked.text: Sources differ on the soil around the roots. For a winter move, one shakes the soil off and replants the rose like a bare-root one, and one says to keep as large a root ball as you can. For a move in the growing season, one says to keep as much soil on the roots as possible.

statements_checked.question: How do I move an established rose?
statements_checked.text: One source says it is very important to keep the roots moist until the rose is replanted. Another waters the soil well the day before the move.

statements_checked.question: How do I move an established rose?
statements_checked.text: Water the rose well once it is replanted, and keep it watered until it recovers. Sources differ on how long: from every day for a week or two, to watering in dry spells through the first year.

statements_checked.question: How do I move an established rose?
statements_checked.text: A rose can be moved in the growing season if you have to. It will need extra watering afterwards. Sources disagree on whether to cut it back first.

statements_checked.question: How do I move an established rose?
statements_checked.text: One source says a rose that has been settled for many years becomes tricky to move. Another lists roses among plants that dislike having their roots disturbed.

statements_checked.question: How do I move an established rose?
statements_checked.text: I couldn't find how often a moved rose survives, or an age beyond which a rose is too old to move. A local rose society is the place to ask.

results.note: Earlier note resolved. The frozen-ground limit is now said and is rightly given as one source (RHS-PL: 'Avoid planting in the middle of winter when the ground is frozen'). The two explanations are on the pages: YAT-NZ 'roses supplied without any soil'; RSNSW-G 'Bare rooted plants are dormant – they have no leaves or flowers'. Dormant-season planting stands at High (RHS-PL, DA-BR, MU in terms; YAT-NZ, GA-2014P, RSSA for winter).

Earlier fail resolved. 'Months are only a guide' is now said, as rules section 4 and the standing decision require for a garden company's month, and 'one garden centre' is right for June (KINGS alone: 'New seasons Roses arrive in store from June'). 'Winter is the best time' is on NZRS-FAQ ('Winter is the best time to plant') and KINGS ('Roses are best planted in winter, however they can be planted right through spring'); PALM-G gives winter through spring. ABG's 'best done in autumn or winter', which the check found is said of container plants, is now recorded under AF-2 and reaches gardeners in the limit of item 6, where it applies. Moderate matches AF-2. Shown in NZ only.

Earlier fail resolved. The statement now leads with the season and the state of the plant (RSSA 'Planting winter bare rooted roses'; RSNSW-G 'Bare rooted plants are dormant ... only available in winter'; GA-2014P 'Because it's winter'), gives the better-supported months first (RSSA 'best done in June or July'; RSNSW-CAL 'planting in June/July'), says 'one source' for May (GA-MAG alone), and says months are only a guide. Moderate matches AF-2. Shown in AU only.

Unchanged, and still passes. It follows RHS-PL ('Plant in late autumn at leaf fall, and from late winter to early spring, before growth resumes'); DA-BR agrees on the outer season. 'Before growth starts' is a check on the plant. Moderate matches AF-3. Shown in GB only.

Earlier note resolved. 'Preferred' is now the pages' own word (CSU 'spring planting is preferred over fall'; MU 'spring planting is preferred'); ISU's 'must be planted in spring' is firmer, and Pip may say less. The -10 °F line and the milder case are both MU and are rightly given as one source ('Where temperatures don't drop below -10 degrees Fahrenheit, either fall or spring planting is satisfactory'). Three US extension voices, Moderate. Shown in US only.

Earlier fail resolved. 'Where winters are cold' is gone; the statement now reports who says what: all year on RHS-PL (UK), YAT-NZ and PALM-G (New Zealand); growing season on MU and CSU (two US sources). The comparison with a bare-root rose is now stated (MU makes it in one sentence). The limit carries the three conditions, each rightly as one source: RHS-PL 'provided the ground is neither frozen, nor very dry'; NZRS-FAQ 'If planting potted roses during spring and summer, keep them well watered'; ABG 'Planting is best done in autumn or winter'. High is kept for the claim in the first sentence only, with the reason recorded in AF-4.

Earlier note resolved. The other seasons are now said: HEIR 'the dormant season in early spring'; UW-PAL 'early spring or late fall'; RHS-MOVE late October to mid-March. 'Not actively growing' is on the pages (NRS-T 'dormant or going dormant, not actively growing'; PALM-FAQ 'dormant with no active growth'). 'Most sources say winter' holds: seven of ten voices. High matches AF-26.

New statement. Every part is on the one page it rests on: PALM-FAQ 'the best time to relocate them would be after pruning in July when the rose is dormant with no active growth' and, in the same answer, 'make sure that the risk of frosts (or freezing weather) has passed'. 'One garden centre' is right, it is shown in NZ only, and it says months are only a guide, so rule 4 and the standing decision on garden companies are met. Low matches AF-28. Two things to know. (a) July and 'once the risk of frost has passed' pull in different directions wherever frosts run on after July; the check recorded that the page 'does not reconcile the two'. The statement repeats both faithfully and Pip cannot settle it, but a gardener in a frosty district is left unsure which to follow. Rule 6's own reason, added to the last sentence, tells them the frost decides and not the month, without adding anything of Pip's. (b) This is a Low statement that is not a precaution. The labels described for the app were High, Moderate, 'Precaution · Low confidence', 'Sources disagree' and 'No source found'; the app needs a plain Low label for it, or it will be shown wrongly.
results.suggested_wording: In New Zealand, one garden centre says the best time to move a rose is after pruning in July, while it is dormant, and once the risk of frost has passed. Months are only a guide, because frosts vary from year to year.

results.note: Same words as item 8 in the first version, which passed. HEIR 'If you need to transplant your rose during the growing season (non-dormant), you can still be successful but water is key!'; DA-MOVE 'it can still be done ... Keep the rose well-watered'; AE-T 'You can still transplant the roses now' with extra water 'through the summer'; TRE-T 'if kept moist it will recover'. Four voices, Moderate.

Earlier note resolved. The bud-union limit is now said, with a plain description that is on the pages (YAT-NZ 'the bumpy bit where the stem joins onto the rootstock'; DA-MOVE 'the swollen area where the rose has been grafted'), and 'differs' rests on AF-20, which is High. Earlier note resolved. It is now limited to a bare-root rose, which is what GA-2019 and CSU are about, and the two single-source positions are each given as one source (MU 'Packaged plants have been pruned and rarely need additional pruning'; RHS-PL 'Prune back in the first winter after planting'). Rightly marked as a disagreement.

Earlier note resolved in full. The above-soil end is now a figure ('up to 5 cm (2 inches) above': YAT-NZ 5 cm, PALM-G 2-5 cm, RSNSW-CAL 3-5 cm, OSU-AE one inch). The below-soil end is right ('10 cm (4 inches)': CSU and ISU, 2 to 4 inches). Both sides' reasons are now given: for burying, cold (ISU 'This helps protect the rose from harsh winter weather'; OSU-AE 'avoidance of cold damage'; MU in context); against, RHS-PL 'reported to increase the risk of rose dieback' and OSU-AE 'In milder climates, disease susceptibility of the graft is a risk'. Marked 'Sources disagree', leads with no side, which is right where the difference follows climate. Remark only: 'dieback' is not explained.

Earlier note resolved: the term is explained and the sentence is now the plain instruction. Earlier fail resolved. results.note: Unchanged, and passed before. Matches RHS-RD ('New plantings may struggle to establish, make poor growth and may even die'), with RHS-FAQ, ARS-RRD and RSSA. Three independent voices; Moderate is right.

Earlier note resolved in full. It now says what to replace the soil with ('fresh soil from another part of the garden': RHS-PL, RHS-RD, RSSA, DA-MOVE), gives the depth (RHS-RD at least 30 cm, RHS-PL 45 cm), puts the old roots correctly (RSSA), and drops 'if you can'. Amounts and the 'one source' count are right. Remark only: the sizes are in centimetres alone, though the statement is shown everywhere and the pages give both ('45cm (18in)', '60cm (2ft)', '30cm (1ft)'); other statements now give both.

Earlier note resolved on three of four points: 'Several' replaces 'Most' (three of five independent voices advise replacing the soil), the specialist's method is now worded as on the page ('well-rotted manure or compost'; 'roses treated with mycorrhizal fungi'), and 'He' is gone. Earlier note resolved. It now says what dormant means in words the pages use ('no active growth', PALM-FAQ; 'not actively growing', NRS-T) and says what the minority say ('late autumn or early spring': HEIR early spring, UW-PAL early spring or late fall, NRS-T late winter to early spring, RHS-MOVE late October to mid-March). 'Most sources say winter' holds for about eight of ten independent voices. High matches AF-26. Identical to PKR-CGD-000016 item 7.

New. Confirmed on PALM-FAQ: 'the best time to relocate them would be after pruning in July when the rose is dormant with no active growth', and 'make sure that the risk of frosts (or freezing weather) has passed'. It is a local month from one garden company, which rule 4 and the standing decision allow: it is shown only in New Zealand, says one garden centre, and says months are only a guide. Low matches AF-28. The page gives July and frost risk together without reconciling them, and the statement repeats both as the page does, adding nothing. Identical to PKR-CGD-000016 item 8. See the package point on the label an ordinary Low statement shows.

This was PKR-CGD-000021 item 2 and passed with a note; the rewording has made it worse. The first sentence still stands (seven independent voices cut back for a dormant move). The range does not (rule 3). (1) The far end is now 'cutting it down to about 30 cm (12 inches)', which is one source, HEIR, and HEIR says 'Cut the rose canes back to 10-12 inches', that is 25 to 30 cm, so the figure shown is only the top of its range. (2) It is not the far end. TUI-T says 'Prune roses back hard before moving' and TUI-Q 'cut it back hard to about 3-5 buds (or nodes) from the graft at ground level'; the earlier wording ('to a hard prune') covered these and the new wording drops them. They are the one New Zealand voice that gives an amount. UW-PAL (three to four canes left) and NRS-T (by half) sit between. So the statement tells a gardener the choices run from a third to 30 cm, when one source cuts harder than that. The term 'hard prune' can be avoided without losing that end.
results.suggested_wording: Cut the top growth back before a winter move. Sources differ on how much: from cutting it back by a third, to cutting it down to 25 to 30 cm (10 to 12 inches), to cutting it right back to 3 to 5 buds above the base.

results.note: This was item 3 and failed; now resolved. The whole of AF-31's range is shown: 'about 25 cm (10 inches) out from the base' (TUI-Q 25-30 cm; UW-PAL one foot) 'to as much as 60 cm (24 inches)' (NRS-T 18 to 24 inches, which the page does not say is a radius or a width, and the statement does not say either), and 'the larger the better' (TRE-T). Keeping the roots is AF-30 as corrected (HEIR, DA-MOVE, NRS-T, KINGS, TRE-T, AE-T). Moderate matches. The soil question is now its own statement (item 5).

New. It answers my earlier package point that the soil conflict reached no gardener, and C-10 is now recorded. Each clause is confirmed: TRE-T, dormant move, 'giving it a shake to release the soil' from the roots and 'You can then plant as a bare root rose'; KINGS, 'dig out as large a root ball as you can manage', said of a move 'best done when dormant during Winter'; TRE-T, growing season, 'keep as much soil around the roots as possible'. Each is said as one source. One against one, so it rightly leads with neither and is marked 'Sources disagree'. NRS-T: 'The day before you transplant your rose bushes, water the soil around the rose bush very well.' Each said as one source; a precaution under rule 7, marked as one, Low shown.

This was item 5; earlier note resolved. It now gives the range of how long: 'every day for a week or two' (HEIR) to dry spells through the first year (RHS-MOVE, DA-MOVE). 'Until it recovers' is KINGS, word for word. The reason High is kept is now recorded on AF-33 (ten voices water at replanting; the RHS supports the whole finding).

New. It answers my earlier package point on AF-34.
